title: Paracelsus
description: Published in 1835 and praised by Wordsworth, Hazlitt and the actor Macready; a dramatic poem on the Renaissance alchemist Paracelsus, whose pursuit of knowledge is set against the claims of love and of common life.
plot_or_argument: Paracelsus seeks universal knowledge and neglects his friends Festus and Michal; he achieves fame as a healer, is denounced, fails, and dies acknowledging that he has missed the truth by seeking it apart from human love, in a death scene of reconciliation.
literary_form: Verse drama in eleven scenes (closet drama)
historical_context: The 1830s vogue for the Renaissance (Bulwer's novels, Carlyle's lectures), the Victorian debate about the claims of knowledge against feeling, and Browning's own ambition to be a poet of the intellectual life.
literary_significance: Paracelsus made Browning's name among the critics and established the Renaissance as his imaginative territory; its theme of the knowledge-seeker who fails through pride is the matrix of the later monologues from 'A Grammarian's Funeral' to 'Andrea del Sarto'.

title: Sordello
description: Published in 1840 and the most notoriously difficult poem of the century — Tennyson said he could make nothing of it, and Browning's readers could not follow its syntax: a poem on the thirteenth-century troubadour Sordello and the politics of Lombardy.
plot_or_argument: Sordello, a poet of Mantua, seeks fame and love; he becomes involved in the Guelf-Ghibelline struggle over the succession of the emperor Frederick II, betrays his trust, and dies in obscurity, having learned that the poet's true work is to make the world's will conscious.
literary_form: Long narrative poem in blank verse
historical_context: The Italian communes of the thirteenth century, Dante's Purgatorio (where Sordello appears), and the Victorian interest in Italian history and in the poet's political role.
literary_significance: Sordello is the extreme case of Browning's difficult middle style, and its failure in the market taught him to write for the voice and for the dramatic moment rather than for the reader of narrative. Its theory of the poet's social function is the philosophical key to his later work.

title: Pippa Passes
description: The first of the Bells and Pomegranates pamphlets, published in 1841: a dramatic poem in four episodes, in which the silk-winder Pippa's songs, overheard by the people of Asolo, change the course of their lives.
plot_or_argument: Pippa, a poor girl of Asolo, is given one holiday a year; her innocent songs, sung as she passes, reform a murderer, prevent a seduction, save a marriage and convert an artist. The four episodes are set simultaneously on the same day.
literary_form: Verse drama (dramatic poem with four episodes)
historical_context: The 1840s and the Victorian idealisation of the pure redeeming woman; the Italian town of Asolo; and the pamphlet form of Bells and Pomegranates, sold cheaply to reach a new public.
literary_significance: Pippa Passes is the most lyrical of Browning's early works and the one in which his faith in the power of art and undesigning goodness is stated most directly; 'The year's at the spring' became one of the best-known Victorian lyrics, and the structure of overheard song influencing action is a technical invention of lasting interest.

title: Dramatic Lyrics
description: Published in 1842 as the third Bells and Pomegranates pamphlet and containing 'My Last Duchess', 'Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister', 'Porphyria's Lover' and 'Johannes Agricola in Meditation': the founding collection of the English dramatic monologue.
plot_or_argument: Each poem is spoken by a dramatic character at a moment of revelation: the Duke of Ferrara exhibits his last duchess's portrait and reveals that he had her killed; the Spanish monk reveals his hatred in the very cadence of his prayer; Porphyria's lover strangles her and is sure God has not said a word.
historical_context: The 1842 pamphlet market, the Victorian fascination with the Italian Renaissance, and the religious revival and its pathologies (the 'madhouse cells' of the two first poems).
literary_significance: Dramatic Lyrics is the collection in which the English dramatic monologue became a distinct genre; 'My Last Duchess' is the most anthologised English poem of the century, and the collection's technique of letting a speaker condemn himself by his own rhetoric is the foundation of the modern poetic exploitation of dramatic voice.

title: Men and Women
description: Published in two volumes in 1855 and a commercial failure — thirteen months after publication 244 copies had been sold — and now regarded as the greatest single volume of Victorian poetry: containing 'Fra Lippo Lippi', 'Andrea del Sarto', 'Bishop Blougram's Apology', 'Cleon', 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came', 'A Toccata of Galuppi's' and 'Love Among the Ruins'.
plot_or_argument: The poems are a gallery of speakers — Renaissance painters, a Greek philosopher, an Elizabethan lover, a bishop, a Roman patrician, a Venetian musician's listener — each caught at the moment when his view of life is revealed as inadequate or heroic. 'Fra Lippo Lippi' defends the flesh against asceticism, 'Andrea del Sarto' is the painter who could do everything but the one thing, 'Bishop Blougram' is the worldly churchman who argues that doubt is a luxury only the faithful can afford.
literary_form: Poetry collection in two volumes (51 poems)
historical_context: The Florence of the 1850s and the Brownings' Italian life, the Victorian crisis of faith and its Catholic and sceptical answers, and the art criticism of the period (Vasari's Lives newly available to English readers).
literary_significance: Men and Women is the central volume of Victorian poetry after In Memoriam: it invented the modern poetic anthology piece, and its speakers' arguments about art, faith and the flesh are the source of the Victorian poetic drama of ideas. Pound, Eliot and the modernist dramatic lyric are inconceivable without it.

title: Dramatis Personae
description: Published in May 1864 and the volume that reversed Browning's neglect, selling 1,700 copies in the first year: containing 'Rabbi Ben Ezra', 'Caliban upon Setebos', 'Mr Sludge, The Medium', 'Abt Vogler', 'Prospice' and 'James Lee's Wife'.
plot_or_argument: The poems range from Caliban's grotesque theology to the spiritualist medium Mr Sludge's self-exposure, from the Rabbi's affirmation of age and love to the widower's defiance of death in 'Prospice'; the collection is organized around the theme of the soul's relation to God and to the beloved.
historical_context: The 1860s, the death of Elizabeth Barrett Browning in 1861 (which shapes 'Prospice' and 'James Lee's Wife'), the vogue of spiritualism in London, and the Oxford Movement's aftermath in the debate on faith.
literary_significance: Dramatis Personae made Browning famous in his own lifetime and contains the poems by which the Victorian religious sensibility is best known; 'Caliban upon Setebos' is the great Victorian poetic treatment of natural theology, and 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' the age's most quoted defence of the imperfect life.

title: The Ring and the Book
description: Published in four volumes in 1868-69 and the longest and most ambitious of Browning's poems: the story of a Roman murder trial of 1698, retold twelve times by the different people involved, until the reader has to weigh the versions.
plot_or_argument: Count Guido Franceschini, a poor nobleman of Arezzo, marries Pompilia, the young ward of a Roman couple, and takes her to Rome, where she is mistreated and flees with the priest Giuseppe Caponsacchi; Guido pursues and murders her and her parents, and is tried and executed. The twelve books give the story in the voices of half Rome, the other half Rome, the tertiary, the murderer, the murdered wife, the young priest, the Pope, and finally the poet's own book.
literary_form: Epic-length narrative poem in twelve books, in blank verse
historical_context: The Old Yellow Book, a printed record of the 1698 trial that Browning bought in a Florence market in 1860, the Italian legal system of the seventeenth century, and the Victorian interest in casuistry and in the relativity of evidence.
literary_significance: The Ring and the Book is the Victorian age's one true epic and the fullest treatment in English of truth as a product of multiple perspectives; its structure anticipates the modernist impersonal narrative (Eliot, Pound, Joyce) and its dramatic psychology is unmatched in Victorian poetry.

title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin; A Child's Story
description: Written for the son of the actor William Macready in 1842 and published in the Hood's Magazine and in the Bells and Pomegranates series the same year: the best-known English retelling of the medieval legend.
plot_or_argument: The town of Hamelin is infested with rats; a mysterious piper offers to remove them for a reward, does so with his music, and is refused payment; he returns and pipes away the children of the town, all but one lame boy who is left behind.
historical_context: The medieval German legend (attested from the thirteenth century), the Victorian children's book market, and the 1840s interest in folk narrative that produced the Grimms' Tales in translation.
literary_significance: The Pied Piper is one of the founding poems of English children's literature and the version in which most English-speakers know the legend; its moral about the consequences of bad faith gave the story its Victorian currency as a parable of the social contract.

title: The Seraphim, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1838 when she was thirty-two: the title poem is a Greek-style drama on the angels who watch the Crucifixion, together with 'The Romaunt of Margaret', 'The Poet's Vow' and the ballads that show the influence of the Greek dramatists she had studied since childhood.
plot_or_argument: The Seraphim stages the angels who witness the Crucifixion and cannot understand God's purpose; the poem is a chorus-driven drama of grief and prophecy. The shorter poems are ballads, romances and meditations on art and the poet's vocation.
historical_context: The 1830s, her reading of Aeschylus and the Greek tragedians, the Italian exile of her father's political sympathies, and the provincial religious culture of Herefordshire.
literary_significance: The Seraphim made her name and shows the classical and prophetic ambition of her early art; it is the volume in which the woman poet claims the Greek dramatic form, and its critical reception opened the way to her appointment as a leading poet of the 1840s.

title: Poems (1844)
description: Published in 1844 and the volume that made her famous: containing 'The Cry of the Children', 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship', 'The Dead Pan', 'Bertha in the Lane' and the first of the sonnets to Robert Browning.
plot_or_argument: 'The Cry of the Children' is a protest against child labour in the mines and factories, written in the metre of a report of the Children's Employment Commission; 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship' is a narrative romance; 'The Dead Pan' narrates the death of the pagan gods; the sonnets record the love that had not yet been spoken.
historical_context: The 1844 report of the Children's Employment Commission, the repeal of the Corn Laws (1846), the anti-slavery movement, and her reading of the Greek and Hebrew poets.
literary_significance: Poems of 1844 is the volume in which the Victorian woman poet became a public political voice; 'The Cry of the Children' is the most famous English poem on child labour, and the volume's reception (and its correspondence with Browning) made it the turning point of her life.

title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
description: Forty-four Petrarchan sonnets written in 1845-46 during the courtship and published in 1850, with the pretence of being translated 'from the Portuguese': the greatest English sonnet sequence of the century by a woman, and the founding text of the Victorian love lyric.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves from the speaker's disbelief that she can be loved, through the growth of love and the fear of losing it, to the marriage and the giving of the child; the central sonnet, 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways', follows 'I never gave a lock of hair away' and precedes the closing sonnets of renewed devotion.
historical_context: The 1845-46 courtship at 50 Wimpole Street, the invalid's seclusion, and the Victorian conventions of the love sonnet, which had been modelled on Petrarch and on the masculine sequence since Wyatt.
literary_significance: Sonnets from the Portuguese gave English poetry its central sequence of reciprocal love and reversed the gender of the Petrarchan tradition: the beloved speaks. 'How do I love thee' is among the most quoted poems in the language, and the sequence is a founding text for the study of Victorian women's writing.

title: Casa Guidi Windows
description: Published in 1851 and written in the apartment in Florence whose windows look on the streets of the 1847-49 revolution: a poem in two parts on Italian liberty, the failure of the 1848-49 risings and the continued hope of the Risorgimento.
plot_or_argument: Part I records the civic festivals of 1847 and the hopes of an Italian nation; Part II, written after the defeat of the Roman Republic and the flight of the Grand Duke, refuses despair and calls on the Italian people to renew the struggle.
literary_form: Two-part political poem in blank verse
historical_context: The 1847-49 Italian revolutions, the flight of Grand Duke Leopold II from Florence, the fall of the Roman Republic in 1849, and the English liberal sympathy for Italy that shaped the Brownings' Florentine years.
literary_significance: Casa Guidi Windows is the finest English poem of the Italian Risorgimento and a major political statement by a woman poet; it broke with the Victorian convention that women's poetry should be domestic and established the public, prophetic voice that Murat and the later poets of liberation emulated.

title: Aurora Leigh
description: Published in November 1856 and the great Victorian poem on the woman artist: the autobiography of a poet, Aurora Leigh, from her childhood in Italy to her mature work and love, and a sustained argument for women's access to art and to meaning.
plot_or_argument: Aurora, orphaned in Florence, is brought up in England by her Puritan aunt, refuses the proposal of her cousin Romney Leigh (who is to be a social reformer), goes to London to write, and publishes her book; Romney's socialist schemes at Leigh Hall fail (the burning of the hall and the death of the people in it), he is blinded, and the novel ends with their marriage on the basis of her art and his repentance.
principal_characters: Aurora Leigh; Romney Leigh; Marian Erle; Lady Waldemar; the aunt; Vincent Carrington; Lord Howe
literary_form: Verse novel in nine books, in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, with a median line of eleven or twelve syllables and an unusually free handling of the iambic base, suited to narrative and argument.
historical_context: The 1850s: the woman question, the 'surplus women' census of 1851, the reforming philanthropies of the 1840s, the position of the woman writer in a market dominated by men, and the Italian exiles of London and Florence.
literary_significance: Aurora Leigh is the first English verse novel by a woman and the central literary argument of the Victorian feminist movement; its heroine is a professional artist, its plot refuses the marriage-ending until the woman has become the equal partner, and its treatment of the social problems of the 1840s (prostitution, poverty, the reformer's failure) is unusually direct. Virginia Woolf's account of it in Second Common Reader (1925) is the standard critical point of departure.

title: Poems before Congress
description: Published in 1860 and dedicated to the Italian exile and patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi: five poems on the politics of Europe in 1859-60 and the independence of Italy, the most openly polemical of Barrett Browning's volumes.
plot_or_argument: The poems address the war of 1859, the cession of Nice and Savoy, the coronation of the king of Italy and the fate of Poland; 'A Curse for a Nation', the volume's best-known poem, was originally written for an American abolitionist society against slavery.
historical_context: The Anglo-French war with Austria, the unification of Italy under Victor Emmanuel and Garibaldi's expedition of 1860, and the anti-slavery agitation in Britain and America.
literary_significance: Poems before Congress is the most politically uncompromising of Barrett Browning's books, and 'A Curse for a Nation' is a major antislavery poem whose misreading as an attack on England caused a scandal. The volume shows the woman poet acting as a commentator on international affairs, a role almost unprecedented in English verse.

title: The Battle of Marathon: A Poem
description: Privately printed in 1820 when she was fourteen, and her first published work: a verse narrative of the Athenian victory over the Persians in 490 BC, written in imitation of Pope's Homer and of the Greek historians.
plot_or_argument: The poem narrates the Persian invasion, the Athenian appeal to Sparta, the Marathon campaign and the victory, with speeches of the Athenian generals and a providential interpretation of the Greek success.
historical_context: The classical education she had shared with her brother Edward, the 1820s taste for epic narrative in verse, and the Greek War of Independence of that year, which gave the poem its topical interest.
literary_significance: The Battle of Marathon is a founding document in the history of women's classical scholarship in English: a fourteen-year-old's imitation of the epic mode that shows both the precocity and the excluded ambition later realised in Aurora Leigh.
attribution_notes: Printed privately in 1820 in an edition of fifty copies for family and friends; the attribution to Elizabeth Barrett Browning is documented by her own references and by the surviving copies.

title: The Bothie of Toper-na-Fuosich: A Long-Vacation Pastoral
description: Published in 1848 (the title later corrected to Tober-na-Vuolich), a 'long-vacation pastoral' in English hexameters: a party of Oxford undergraduates reading in the Scottish Highlands, and the decision of one of them to marry a Highland girl and emigrate.
plot_or_argument: Philip Hewson, a radical undergraduate, falls in love with the peasant girl Elspie Mackaye and, rejecting the conventional options of the educated man, marries her and emigrates to New Zealand, where the poem's epilogue shows him as a settler and a democrat.
historical_context: The 1848 revolutions, the Oxford of the Tractarian crisis and the undergraduate reading party, the Scottish Highlands after the Clearances, and the emigration schemes of the later 1840s.
literary_significance: The Bothie is the first English poem to use hexameters for a sustained modern narrative and the first Victorian poem to treat marriage across class as a serious democratic choice; it is the crucial link between the Victorian long poem and the modernist verse novel.

title: Amours de Voyage
description: Written in 1849 during the siege of Rome and published in the Atlantic Monthly in 1858: a verse novel in letters, in which the English tourist Claude's indecision prevents him from declaring his love, and the 1849 Roman Republic falls in the background.
plot_or_argument: Claude, travelling in Italy with his family, meets Mary Trevellyn; their courtship is conducted in letters and in mutual hesitations, and Claude's inability to commit, together with the disruption of the siege of Rome, separates them for good; the poem ends with his solitary departure and an epilogue in which the Trevellyns have gone home.
historical_context: The Roman Republic of 1849 and the French siege of Rome, the English tourist in Italy, and the Victorian crisis of religious belief that makes Claude's paralysis both temperamental and intellectual.
literary_significance: Amours de Voyage is the most modern of Victorian poems: a comedy of indecision in which the hero's scepticism is diagnosed rather than celebrated, and its epistolary-hexameter form is a permanent model for the verse novel. It is also one of the best poems in English on the 1848 revolutions.

title: Dipsychus
description: Written in Venice in 1850 and published posthumously in 1865: a dramatic poem in which the earnest, divided Dipsychus is tempted by the cynical Spirit of the world through the streets, canals and churches of Venice.
plot_or_argument: Dipsychus, an idealist, is accompanied by a Spirit who argues for pleasure, compromise and the acceptance of the world as it is; the poem moves through Venice's carnival, a ball, a church and the lagoon, and ends without resolving the argument, in a chorus of resignation.
literary_form: Dramatic poem in blank verse and lyrics (posthumous)
historical_context: Venice in 1850 under Austrian rule, the Victorian debate between earnestness and worldliness, and the 'spirit of the age' as a literary commonplace of the 1840s-50s.
literary_significance: Dipsychus is the most sophisticated Victorian treatment of the divided self in dramatic form, and its Spirit is the ancestor of the ironic tempter in modern verse drama; its uncompleted state and its refusal of a moral answer make it a key document of Victorian scepticism.

title: The Latest Decalogue
description: Published posthumously in 1862: a ten-couplet parody of the Ten Commandments that reduces each to its commercial and social equivalent, and the most quoted Victorian epigram.
plot_or_argument: Each couplet restates a commandment in the language of Victorian respectability and self-interest: 'Thou shalt not kill; but needst not strive / Officiously to keep alive'; 'Thou shalt not steal; an empty feat, / When it's so lucrative to cheat'.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s and the Victorian compromise of commercial Christianity; the epigram was not published in Clough's lifetime and appeared in the 1862 Poems and remains his best-known single poem.
literary_significance: The Latest Decalogue is the most concentrated Victorian critique of the commercial corruption of religion and one of the founding texts of the modern ironic epigram; its lines on 'the Decalogue' entered the language and are still quoted as the epitome of Victorian hypocrisy.

title: Mari Magno
description: Clough's last long poem, written on his final voyage and published posthumously in 1862: five tales told by passengers on a transatlantic steamer, on love, marriage, money and death.
plot_or_argument: A group of travellers tell stories to pass the voyage: the first on a marriage prevented by money, the second on a wife's death, the third on a seduction and its consequences, the fourth on a sailor's love, the fifth on a death at sea. The frame and the tales together make an argument about the moral luck of love and marriage.
historical_context: The transatlantic passage of 1861 and the emigrant culture of the period, the Victorian debate on marriage and money, and Clough's own failing health.
literary_significance: Mari Magno is the most humane and least known of Clough's long poems, and its frame-narrative of travellers' tales gives the Victorian debate on marriage a genuinely popular form; it is the best introduction to the late Clough.

title: The Strayed Reveller, and Other Poems
description: Published anonymously in 1849 as the work of 'A', and the volume that contains 'The Forsaken Merman', 'Mycerinus', 'The Sick King in Bokhara' and 'Resignation': the poetry of withdrawal, of the classical mask and of resignation before the world.
plot_or_argument: 'The Strayed Reveller' is a dialogue between the young reveller and Circe, in which the poet's vision is purchased by exclusion from action; 'The Forsaken Merman' is a ballad of a sea-creature's wife who leaves him for her church; 'Mycerinus' is the Egyptian king who learns that he has only six years to live and turns them into pleasure.
historical_context: The 1848 revolutions and the failure of the Oxford hopes, the death of Arnold's father and his own religious crisis, and the classical reading of Balliol.
literary_significance: The Strayed Reveller established Arnold's characteristic subject — the modern mind's exile from the world of action and belief — and its title poem is the most complete statement of his theory of the poet's position. The anonymity signalled the volume's difference from the Victorian earnestness of its contemporaries.

title: Empedocles on Etna, and Other Poems
description: Published anonymously in 1852 with 'Tristram and Iseult', 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (added in 1853), 'Memorial Versions' and the 'Switzerland' lyrics, including 'To Marguerite'. The title poem was withdrawn by Arnold from the 1853 collection.
plot_or_argument: Empedocles, the Sicilian philosopher, has lost the power to think and act; he converses with Pausanias and with Callicles, whose songs celebrate the world he can no longer enter, and climbs Etna to throw himself into the crater. The lyrics 'The Scholar-Gipsy' and 'To Marguerite' dramatise the same estrangement in modern English terms.
historical_context: The 1850s and the Victorian crisis of faith; the Greek philosopher's suicide as an image of the modern intellectual's despair; the poem's withdrawal from the 1853 Poems because it offered no remedy, only a 'dialogue of the mind with itself'.
literary_significance: Empedocles on Etna is the central English poem of Victorian unbelief and the work in which Arnold's classical method and his modern melancholy meet; the Preface to the 1853 Poems, in which he explained its withdrawal, is one of the founding documents of modern criticism, and the poem's portrait of the intellectual's isolation is the direct ancestor of the modernist long poem of the divided mind.

title: Poems (1853)
description: Published in 1853 under Arnold's own name, with the famous Preface on the choice of subjects, and reissued in a second series in 1855: the collection that made him the poet of Victorian doubt and the critic of the age.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Sohrab and Rustum', 'The Scholar-Gipsy', 'The Church of Brou', 'The Forsaken Merman', 'Tristram and Iseult' and the 'Switzerland' poems, together with the Preface's argument that poetry must choose actions and subjects of permanent interest rather than the modern 'dialogue of the mind with itself'.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Crimean War, and Arnold's double life as school inspector and poet; the Preface answers the charge that his poetry was too purely personal and too melancholy.
literary_significance: The 1853 Poems is the volume in which the Victorian critical revolution began: its Preface put the choice of subject at the centre of criticism and defined the modern poet's problem as the absence of a living mythology, and its poems supplied the age with its central images of isolation and of the 'darkling plain'.

title: Sohrab and Rustum
description: Published in the 1853 Poems and generally regarded as Arnold's finest narrative poem: a story from the Persian epic the Shahnameh, in which a father unknowingly kills his son in single combat.
plot_or_argument: Rustum, the Persian hero, has a son Sohrab by the princess Tahminah; Sohrab, seeking his father, joins the Tartar army and challenges the Persian champion, and in the duel Rustum wounds him mortally before discovering the truth. The poem ends with the father's grief on the banks of the Oxus.
historical_context: The Victorian interest in the East (the Shahnameh, the 1850s oriental scholarship), the imperial frontier wars of the period, and Arnold's theory of the permanently interesting subject.
literary_significance: Sohrab and Rustum is the finest English narrative poem of the 1850s and the work in which Arnold's classical ideal is fully realised: it was written in deliberate imitation of Homer and gave Victorian poetry a model of the objective narrative that the age's criticism demanded.

title: The Scholar-Gipsy
description: Published in the 1853 Poems and one of the most influential lyrics of the century: the legend of the Oxford student who joined the gipsies to learn their secret, transferred to a meditation on the modern world's 'strange disease of modern life'.
plot_or_argument: The speaker recalls the seventeenth-century scholar who left Oxford for the gipsies and asks whether he still walks the Oxfordshire countryside; the poem turns from the legend to the contrast between the scholar's single-minded quest and the 'sick hurry' of modern life, ending with the wish that the scholar may never be caught by the modern world.
historical_context: The Oxfordshire landscape of Arnold's youth, the 1850s railway and the 'strange disease of modern life', and the seventeenth-century source in Glanvill's Vanity of Dogmatizing.
literary_significance: The Scholar-Gipsy is the central English poem of the modern intellectual's nostalgia for a unified life, and its closing description of the 'darkling plain' of modern existence (developed in 'Dover Beach') gave the Victorian age its most quoted diagnosis of itself. It is a foundation text for the criticism of modernity.
